title: Penny and Saffron's Blanket Adventure
markdown:
It was a soft morning in the sun-dappled bedroom. Light peeked through the curtains like a sleepy kitten and painted golden stripes across the rug. Toys lay in their favourite spots. The air hummed with quiet.

Penny the penguin plush lay on the Big Green Bed, stitches neat as a row of tiny peas, round body soft. Beside him Saffron the rabbit stirred, ears like velvety petals. Their little person stirred too. But there was no happy hum. There was a sniffle. A tiny sound that made the quiet feel thin.

“Oh dear,” whispered Penny. His felt tummy gave a concerned bounce. “What’s the matter?”

The little person sat up, brow crinkled like a rumpled handkerchief. “My blanket,” they mumbled. “My special cozy blanket is gone. It’s not here.”

Penny’s felt heart fluttered. His flippers felt too clumsy for helping. Saffron’s ears drooped, not with her own sadness, but with care. Her busy nose went still.

“Gone?” squeaked Saffron. “It’s always right here. Soft and warm.”

They looked at the bed. The green cover was rumpled. The pillow had a Penny-shaped dent. No blue blanket. No cozy.

“We need a plan,” said Saffron, firm and gentle. “We must map the whole bedroom. Every corner. Every sneaky place.”

Penny nodded so hard he nearly tumbled off the bed. “A map. Then we won’t miss a spot.”

Saffron found a clean white paper that had fallen from the art table. Penny wriggled under the bed and came back with a stubby bright-blue crayon, dusty with fluff.

“First the Big Green Bed,” said Saffron. Her ears pointed like little pencils. She sketched a large rectangle, careful and slow. “That’s where we started.”

Penny watched, button eyes wide. He wanted to draw too. He took the crayon. He tried a toy car on the bed. His flippers were not made for fine lines. The car came out a wiggly blue worm. Or perhaps a happy caterpillar.

“Oh, Saffron,” he sighed. “Mine looks all wrong.”

Saffron paused. She did not want Penny’s crayon to feel like a mistake. She remembered how he always tried.

“Yours is a special journey car,” she said. “Maybe the blanket went on a journey too. Your car can show the way.”

Penny’s eyes twinkled. He drew another wiggly blue line beside the rectangle, a path for the car to follow. “A journey car.”

They mapped on. Saffron drew the tall bookshelf with its colourful stories. Penny added a wobbly circle for the bouncy ball that liked to roll off. They drew the snack table, and the comfy armchair for quiet stories. Penny’s lines stayed wiggly. Saffron’s stayed neat. The paper began to look like their room, only smaller and bluer.

Then they used the map. That was the point of a map.

They checked under the Big Green Bed, where the crayon had lived. Dust-fluff. A lost sock. No blanket. They checked the armchair, lifting a cushion as big as Penny. A crumb. A button. No blanket. At the snack table Saffron’s nose found yesterday’s apple smell and nothing blue. Penny peered into the toy basket. Blocks stared back. The little person watched from the pillows, lip still wobbly, hoping without interrupting.

“Where could the blanket be?” Penny mused, tilting his plush head. “Maybe it wanted sunshine. A little nap somewhere sunny.”

Saffron’s nose twitched. She pointed to her window on the map. “Sunshine comes through there. But the window is high. The blanket is too big to fly.”

They looked at the window anyway, because maps like to be thorough. Stripes of gold. No blue. They looked up, up, up. At the very top of the bookshelf, behind a pile of books, a tiny corner of familiar soft blue peeked out.

“My blanket,” squeaked Penny.

The shelf was much too high. Saffron stretched. Her long ears reached. Not enough. Penny bounced. He only wobbled on the rug and sat down with a soft pfump.

They were so close. The blue waited, like a secret that had climbed.

Saffron’s ears gave a worried droop. Then she saw Penny’s journey car on the map, still wiggly, still going. She looked at the long bright-red toy train on the floor, wheels still.

“The train,” she whispered. “It’s long. Like a reaching arm.”

Penny’s buttons lit. “A reaching arm.”

Together they nudged the train toward the bookshelf. Saffron pushed with her nose. Penny wiggled his flippers and steadied the carriages so the red engine would not wander off toward the toy car instead. Inch by inch the engine arrived beneath the high shelf. The carpet rasped. A book on the lowest shelf watched them with a closed mouth. The train smelled faintly of dust and yesterday’s play.

“I’ll stand on the engine,” said Saffron. “You stand on the last carriage. That will make us a little taller.”

Penny climbed onto the last carriage. It wobbled. He held his flippers tight. The wheels gave a tiny tick. Saffron hopped onto the engine. Her ears brushed a book spine. Together they were higher. Almost high enough. Saffron stretched her paw. The rough carpet was far below. She heard Penny’s soft wiggles on the last car. Penny stretched his flipper. The blue fabric looked so soft, just out of reach, as if it had only climbed up for a better view of the morning.

They nudged the corner. Gentle. Once. The blanket did not come. Saffron tried again, a little braver. Penny leaned, clumsy flippers and all. The blanket teetered. Then it tumbled down onto the rug, landing as softly as a feather.

The little person gasped. They scrambled from the bed and ran to the blanket, hugging it, burying their face in the familiar warmth. A smile chased the sniffle away. They sat right there on the rug for a moment, blanket tented over their head like a small blue morning, and then they laughed because the tent was silly and the blanket was found.

Penny and Saffron looked at each other. The Big Green Bed was still there. The map still showed a wiggly blue car. The little person climbed back up, blanket and all, and tucked the blue around Penny’s round side and Saffron’s velvety ears, and the golden stripes on the rug looked like themselves again.

They giggled, a bright sound, and hugged Penny, and hugged Saffron, and the bedroom hummed with quiet peace, only now the peace had a blue edge, and it was home.
